title: TH_EX1: Visually driven survey analysis of student learning outcomes
text:
Data Description
Variables follow the codebook structure and are grouped into two blocks. Group A covers demographics, background characteristics, time allocation, and the outcome. It includes year of study, gender, policy beneficiary status, minority status, poor household status, time spent with friends, time spent on social media, time spent studying, and GPA. Group B contains nine Likert items that describe learning adaptation and perceived supports. Each item is recorded on a five point scale from 1 to 5.

title: TH_EX1: Visually driven survey analysis of student learning outcomes
text:
Analytical Questions
The analysis begins with a descriptive overview of the GPA distribution and the sample composition by key demographics. It then compares GPA patterns across year and gender using effect size summaries that remain interpretable under sample imbalance. Next, it examines descriptive associations between background disadvantage indicators and GPA. It also studies how time allocation relates to GPA while respecting the ordinal nature of the time categories. The report then evaluates whether the nine support and adaptation Likert items vary systematically across GPA levels. Finally, it fits an ordinal regression model to summarise how GPA relates jointly to background, time allocation, and perceived supports within a single multivariable framework.

Data Wrangling
This section recodes integer codes into ordered factors following the codebook. GPA is treated as an ordinal outcome with five ordered categories. The nine Likert items are also treated as ordinal variables on a one to five scale. Time allocation variables are ordinal by construction and are retained as ordered factors for descriptive visualisations. For the multivariable model, time allocation is additionally represented as a numeric index to reduce parameter complexity while preserving ordering.
Quality checks include missingness summaries, range checks for GPA and Likert items, and validation of unused factor levels that may produce unstable or rank deficient design matrices in ordinal regression.

section: Observation section: Overall GPA distribution and sample structure
text:
Observation section: Overall GPA distribution and sample structure


Code
gpa_dist<-df|>count(gpa)|>mutate(p=n/sum(n),label=paste0("n=",n,"   ",scales::percent(p,accuracy=0.1)))
p1<-ggplot(gpa_dist,aes(gpa,p,fill=gpa))+geom_col(width=0.75,alpha=0.9)+geom_text(aes(label=label),vjust=-0.4,size=3)+
  scale_x_discrete(labels=\(x) stringr::str_wrap(x,10))+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent_format(accuracy=1),expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.12)))+
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option="C",end=0.9,guide="none")+labs(title="GPA distribution",x=NULL,y="Share of students")+theme_survey()+
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(lineheight=0.95))
comp_long<-df|>mutate(across(c(year,gender,poor_stu,policy_stu,minority_stu),as.character))|>
  pivot_longer(cols=c(year,gender,poor_stu,policy_stu,minority_stu),names_to="dimension",values_to="group")|>
  count(dimension,group)|>group_by(dimension)|>mutate(p=n/sum(n),label=paste0("n=",n,"   ",scales::percent(p,accuracy=0.1)))|>ungroup()|>
  mutate(dimension=fct_recode(dimension,"Year"="year","Gender"="gender","Poor household"="poor_stu","Policy beneficiary"="policy_stu","Minority"="minority_stu"))
p2<-ggplot(comp_long,aes(group,p,fill=group))+geom_col(width=0.7,alpha=0.9)+geom_text(aes(label=label),vjust=-0.5,size=3)+
  facet_wrap(~dimension,ncol=2,scales="free_x")+
  scale_x_discrete(labels=\(x) stringr::str_wrap(x,10))+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent_format(accuracy=1),expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.18)))+
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option="C",end=0.85,guide="none")+labs(title="Sample structure",x=NULL,y="Share within dimension")+theme_survey()+
  theme(panel.spacing=grid::unit(1.2,"lines"),strip.text=element_text(size=11),axis.text.x=element_text(size=10,lineheight=0.95))
(p1|p2)+plot_layout(widths=c(1.05,2.35))









The GPA distribution concentrates in the middle categories, with relatively few observations in the lowest and highest categories. The sample is also strongly imbalanced across year and gender, which affects the precision of group comparisons. Smaller groups yield wider uncertainty and are more sensitive to sampling noise. Background indicators show additional imbalance, especially minority status, where the smaller group size limits precision. Subsequent sections therefore prioritise effect size summaries and uncertainty displays rather than relying on raw differences in bar heights.

Observation section: GPA differences by year and gender


Code
prop_ci <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  p <- mean(x)
  se <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
  tibble(p = p, lo = p - 1.96 * se, hi = p + 1.96 * se, n = n)
}
g_year <- df |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(prop_ci(high_gpa), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(dimension = "Year", group = as.character(year))
g_gender <- df |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarise(prop_ci(high_gpa), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(dimension = "Gender", group = as.character(gender))
g_plot <- bind_rows(g_year, g_gender) |>
  mutate(dimension = factor(dimension, levels = c("Year", "Gender")))
ggplot(g_plot, aes(x = group, y = p)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = pmax(0, lo), ymax = pmin(1, hi)), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n=", n)), vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ dimension, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of Good or Excellent GPA by year and gender",
    subtitle = "Point estimates with approximate 95 percent intervals highlight imbalance and uncertainty",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share with GPA at least Good"
  ) +
  theme_survey()









Year and gender differences are summarised using a common effect size, the share of students with GPA at least Good. This framing supports direct comparisons across groups even when the sample is unbalanced. Interval widths vary substantially because group sample sizes differ, so apparent gaps must be interpreted together with uncertainty. These results are descriptive associations within the observed sample and motivate the use of multivariable summaries later in the report.


Observation section: Background inequalities using poor, policy, minority


Code

geom_text(aes(label=paste0("n=",n)),vjust=-0.8,size=3)+
facet_wrap(~dimension,ncol=3)+

p3









The three background indicators show descriptive differences in the share of high GPA. Students from poor households tend to have a lower share of high GPA than those not in poor households. Policy beneficiary status also differs in high GPA share. Minority status exhibits the widest uncertainty because the minority group is much smaller. These patterns describe observed associations and do not identify causal mechanisms, but they provide context for later multivariable modelling. ### Observation section: Time allocation versus GPA

time_long<-df|>mutate(across(all_of(time_vars),as.numeric))|>pivot_longer(all_of(time_vars),names_to="dimension",values_to="time_cat")|>group_by(dimension,time_cat)|>summarise(n=n(),p=mean(high_gpa),se=sqrt(p*(1-p)/n),lo=p-1.96*se,hi=p+1.96*se,.groups="drop")|>mutate(time_index=as.numeric(time_cat),dimension=fct_recode(dimension,"Time with friends"="time_friends","Time on social media"="time_socical_media","Time spent studying"="time_studying"))

Time allocation variables are recorded as ordered categories, so the horizontal axis represents ordered bins rather than equal hour differences. Studying time is concentrated toward higher categories in this sample, which reduces contrast for some comparisons. Social media time shows a clearer descriptive pattern in which the highest category aligns with a lower share of high GPA. Time with friends shows smaller differences with substantial interval overlap. These findings remain descriptive summaries of ordinal categories and support including time allocation jointly with background and supports in the ordinal regression. ### Observation section: Perceived supports and learning adaptation

Across the nine Likert items, mean scores tend to increase with higher GPA levels, suggesting a consistent descriptive gradient between perceived supports or learning adaptation and academic outcome. The heatmap fixes the colour scale to the full one to five range so comparisons remain meaningful across items. The composite support index complements item level patterns by summarising overall support, while the distribution plots highlight overlap between GPA groups and heterogeneity within groups. Likert summaries are interpreted descriptively with the ordinal scale in mind.


Observation section: Multivariable summary with ordinal regression


Code
df_model <- df |>
  transmute(
    gpa = gpa,
    year = year,
    gender = gender,
    poor_stu = poor_stu,
    policy_stu = policy_stu,
    minority_stu = minority_stu,
    time_friends_i = as.numeric(time_friends),
    time_social_i = as.numeric(time_socical_media),
    time_study_i = as.numeric(time_studying),
    support_z = support_z
  ) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    across(where(is.factor), ~ droplevels(.x))
  )

m_polr <- polr(
  gpa ~ year + gender + poor_stu + policy_stu + minority_stu +
    time_friends_i + time_social_i + time_study_i + support_z,
  data = df_model,
  Hess = TRUE,
  method = "logistic"
)

coefs <- coef(summary(m_polr)) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("term") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(estimate = Value, se = `Std. Error`) |>
  mutate(
    lo = estimate - 1.96 * se,
    hi = estimate + 1.96 * se,
    or = exp(estimate),
    or_lo = exp(lo),
    or_hi = exp(hi)
  ) |>
  filter(!str_detect(term, "\\|"))

ggplot(coefs, aes(x = or, y = fct_reorder(term, or))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = or_lo, xmax = or_hi), linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Ordinal regression summary as odds ratios",
    subtitle = "Values above 1 align with higher GPA categories under the model, uncertainty shown as intervals",
    x = "Odds ratio on log scale",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_survey()









The ordinal regression model summarises conditional associations between GPA and multiple covariates simultaneously under the proportional odds framework. Results are reported as odds ratios, where values above 1 indicate alignment with higher GPA categories after conditioning on other covariates. The support index shows a positive association with GPA, while higher social media time shows a negative association in this sample when other variables are held constant. Interval widths communicate estimation uncertainty, and wide intervals indicate limited precision under sample imbalance. These results describe conditional associations and do not establish causality. ## Visual Design Considerations Visual choices prioritise interpretability under imbalance and ordinal measurement. Comparable charts use consistent y axis ranges where appropriate, and Likert colour scales are fixed to the one to five range to support cross item comparison. Composition charts include both counts and percentages so readers can audit sample imbalance directly from the figure. Ordered factors follow substantive meaning rather than alphabetical ordering. A colourblind safe viridis palette is used consistently, and annotations are used only when they reduce reading time, such as counts on group summaries and a reference line at odds ratio 1 in the regression plot.

title: TH_EX1: Visually driven survey analysis of student learning outcomes
text:
Key Findings
Overall distribution and structure. GPA concentrates in the middle categories, and the sample is heavily imbalanced by year and gender, so uncertainty varies widely across group comparisons. Year and gender patterns. Year groups show larger differences in the share of high GPA than gender groups, and group sample sizes strongly influence interval widths. Background indicators. Poor household, policy beneficiary, and minority indicators are associated with lower high GPA share, with minority estimates showing the lowest precision due to small group size. Time allocation. Social media time shows the clearest negative association at the highest category, while studying time shows limited contrast because responses concentrate in higher categories. Perceived supports. Likert item means and the composite support index increase across GPA categories, with substantial overlap that indicates heterogeneity rather than strict separation. Multivariable summary. In the ordinal regression, support index is positively associated with higher GPA categories and social media time is negatively associated, while background indicators remain relevant after joint conditioning, with uncertainty varying across terms.

title: TH_EX1: Visually driven survey analysis of student learning outcomes
text:
Limitations
All measures are self reported and may reflect recall bias and social desirability effects. GPA, time allocation, and Likert items are ordinal, so analyses avoid treating them as interval scale quantities. The sample is imbalanced by year and gender, which affects precision and limits generalisability. Associations may reflect unmeasured confounding, including prior preparation, programme differences, and motivation. The multivariable model summarises conditional associations under the proportional odds assumption, and interpretation remains associational.
